introduction.heading: What Is HTTP?
introduction.description: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the language browsers and servers use to talk to each other. Every time a page loads, a button triggers a fetch, or an app checks for new data, a client sends an HTTP request and a server sends back an HTTP response. Node.js can speak both sides of that conversation - it can be the server handling requests (as you saw with the built-in http module) and, through the Fetch API, the client sending them. This page covers the rest of the picture: how requests and responses are structured, how REST APIs are commonly designed around them, and the browser APIs - Fetch, AbortController, WebSockets, and Server-Sent Events - used to talk to them from client-side JavaScript.

concepts.title: Request & Response
concepts.description: A client sends a request (method, URL, headers, optional body); a server sends back a response (status code, headers, optional body). Every HTTP interaction is one round trip of this cycle

concepts.title: Methods
concepts.description: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE signal intent - reading data, creating it, replacing it, partially updating it, or removing it

concepts.title: Status Codes
concepts.description: A three-digit number in the response that summarizes what happened: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error

concepts.title: Headers
concepts.description: Key/value metadata sent with a request or response - content type, authorization, caching rules, and more - separate from the body

concepts.title: Cookies
concepts.description: Small pieces of state a server asks the browser to store via a Set-Cookie header, which the browser then re-attaches automatically on later requests to that origin

concepts.title: CORS
concepts.description: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing - a browser security mechanism that blocks a page from reading responses from a different origin unless the server explicitly allows it

concepts.title: REST
concepts.description: An architectural style that maps CRUD operations onto HTTP methods and URLs representing resources, e.g. GET /users/7 or DELETE /posts/3

concepts.title: JSON
concepts.description: JavaScript Object Notation - the de facto data format for API request and response bodies, parsed with JSON.parse and produced with JSON.stringify

lifecycle.heading: The Request/Response Cycle
lifecycle.description: Behind a single fetch() call, several things happen in order: the browser resolves the domain to an IP address (DNS), opens a connection to the server (TCP, plus a TLS handshake for HTTPS), sends the request line, headers, and body, waits while the server processes it, and finally receives the response line, headers, and body back. Fetch (and the browser) handle all of this for you - but knowing the steps makes it much easier to reason about latency, caching, and why a request might fail before it ever reaches your server code.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started
steps: Open any site's DevTools Network tab and reload the page - every request/response pair is right there: method, status, headers, and body
Try fetch("https://api.example.com") in the browser console - it returns a Promise that resolves to a Response object
Call response.json() (also a Promise) to parse the body as JSON once the response arrives
Wrap fetch in try/catch and check response.ok - fetch only rejects on network failure, not on 4xx/5xx status codes
Reach for a public test API like jsonplaceholder.typicode.com when you want to practice REST calls without running your own server

fullExample.heading: Full Example, Step by Step
fullExample.title: A real-world fetch: headers, JSON, errors, and a timeout
fullExample.description: This ties the concepts above together in one realistic function. Click through the steps to see which lines each one is talking about.

steps.label: Create an AbortController
steps.explanation: An AbortController gives you a signal you can trigger later. Here it's paired with setTimeout so the request cancels itself if the server takes longer than 5 seconds.

steps.label: Call fetch with options
steps.explanation: fetch's second argument configures the request: method, headers (including Authorization for authenticated routes), and the abort signal that lets this request be cancelled.

steps.label: Check response.ok
steps.explanation: fetch only rejects on network-level failures (offline, DNS, CORS). A 404 or 500 still resolves successfully - response.ok (true only for 2xx) is how you catch those yourself.

steps.label: Parse the JSON body
steps.explanation: response.json() is itself async - it reads and parses the response stream, so it needs its own await.

steps.label: Distinguish abort from other errors
steps.explanation: When a request is aborted, fetch rejects with an error whose name is "AbortError" - checking for it lets you tell a deliberate cancellation apart from a real failure.

steps.label: Always clear the timer
steps.explanation: finally runs whether the request succeeded, failed, or was aborted, so the timeout never fires late and aborts a request that already finished.
